cases.dilemmas: (i) Public interest in exposing hidden phone tracking versus a vendor's claim of confidentiality. (ii) Should privacy findings about software users can't remove go straight to the public? (iii) What changed the outcome: the law, or public pressure?

cases.summary: Webster found a direct object reference flaw in his pension fund's website exposing other members' information and reported it. First State Super reported him to police and threatened further legal action, then withdrew the threat after negative publicity.
cases.dilemmas: (i) How many other members' records is it acceptable to view to show a flaw is real? (ii) Should a fund be able to make the reporter pay for its own security failures? (iii) Does public pressure, rather than law, end up deciding these cases?

cases.institution: Brenno de Winter / Trans Link Systems (OV-chipkaart)
cases.summary: De Winter, a journalist, reported on flaws in the Dutch OV-chipkaart transit payment system. A criminal complaint followed and he was questioned; the government took legal action against him for covering the issue.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should journalists demonstrate a transit-card flaw themselves to prove a story? (ii) Is prosecuting a reporter a proportionate response to fare fraud risk? (iii) Where is the line between investigative journalism and exploitation?

cases.summary: Researchers reported a buffer overflow in Magix Music Maker 16 and were threatened under Germany's anti-hacking law. They published anyway and persuaded Magix to change its stance; Magix opened a researcher portal whose terms bar disclosure before a fix.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is a vendor portal that forbids disclosure until a fix exists a step forward or a gag? (ii) Should researchers accept programs whose terms remove their timeline? (iii) Did publishing under threat help future researchers or only this case?

cases.summary: Roth built a password-cracking tool running on Amazon EC2. His apartment was raided, his bank account frozen, and he was kept from releasing the tool at Black Hat DC; the injunction was later revoked and he published the research.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Releasing a cheap, cloud-based cracking tool: defensive awareness or attacker uplift? (ii) Are raids and frozen accounts proportionate responses to a planned talk? (iii) Should dual-use tools be released openly or to vetted users only?

cases.institution: Hari Prasad / ECIL Electronic Voting Machines (India)
cases.summary: Prasad co-authored a 2010 paper showing vulnerabilities in India's electronic voting machines. Mumbai police arrested him and pressed him to reveal the anonymous source who provided the machine; he spent seven days in custody before release on bail. disclose.io also lists the case among incidents that crossed the line because the machine was allegedly stolen.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is research on an improperly obtained voting machine justified by the public interest in election integrity? (ii) Should researchers protect an anonymous source at personal legal risk? (iii) Does government pressure on election-security research undermine or protect public trust?

cases.institution: Varun Uppal & Gyan Chawdhary / Financial Industry Client
cases.summary: A talk on hacking high-speed trading systems was pulled from a security conference under financial pressure, the potential loss of a client, and was never presented elsewhere.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should a firm's client relationships decide whether research is published? (ii) Do markets benefit more from silence or from disclosure of trading-system flaws? (iii) Who represents the public interest when the only objector is a paying customer?

cases.summary: Huang's Black Hat 2010 talk, an archaeological study of China's government-backed hacking from 2001 to 2010, was cancelled two weeks before the conference due to pressure from the Taiwanese government.
cases.dilemmas: (i) When geopolitical concerns conflict with research publication, whose interests should prevail? (ii) Should researchers comply with pressure from a government that isn't their direct regulator? (iii) Does suppressing threat-actor research help or harm defenders?

cases.institution: Scott Jarkoff (TechMiso) / RSA (Navy Federal Credit Union)
cases.summary: Jarkoff's site published a report on security issues with Navy Federal Credit Union's website. RSA challenged the publication, and RSA backed down after TechMiso and its host pushed back.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should a security vendor act to suppress reporting about a client's website? (ii) Is publishing first justified when a financial institution's members are exposed? (iii) What role should hosting providers play when pressured to remove research?

cases.summary: James published XSS and phishing vulnerabilities on Comerica Bank's website. Comerica sent a cease-and-desist to Tumblr, which removed the information while the vulnerability remained present.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Removing the report while the flaw stays live: who does that protect? (ii) Should platforms honor takedowns of security research about unpatched flaws? (iii) Was public-first disclosure appropriate for a phishing-enabling bank flaw?

cases.summary: HackersBlog published multiple vulnerabilities and intrusions affecting Orange.fr and later reported apparent legal threats, without publishing their details.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is publishing evidence of intrusions into a telecom's systems research or a breach? (ii) Do unpublished legal threats deserve the same weight as documented ones? (iii) How should groups that access data to prove flaws be judged?

cases.summary: Sequoia threatened legal action over a planned independent examination of its voting machines, and a judge suppressed the resulting report on voting machine security; as of October 2008 it remained unpublished.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should voting machine vendors be able to block independent examination of systems used in public elections? (ii) Trade-secret claims versus voters' right to know. (iii) Should researchers accept engagements that a vendor can veto?

cases.summary: Secunia published vulnerabilities in Autonomy's KeyView after Autonomy threatened legal action. Autonomy reportedly threatened CORE Security as well, which was not made public.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should researchers publicize threats they receive, or handle them quietly? (ii) Is it fair to the field when one firm resists a threat and another stays silent? (iii) Can legal threats against a widely embedded library ever serve its downstream users?

cases.summary: Halvar Flake was denied entry into the United States on his way to teach security training, and the training was cancelled at the last minute.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should border authorities be able to block researchers from sharing defensive knowledge? (ii) How should international researchers weigh travel risk when presenting in other countries? (iii) Do conferences owe foreign speakers legal and logistical support?

cases.summary: Karunaratne published information about a backdoor in routers supplied by his ISP, Be Unlimited. The ISP terminated his service; passwords were redacted, a patch was supplied, and his service had not been restored as of July 2007.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is publishing details of an ISP router backdoor justified when every customer is exposed? (ii) Is cutting off a customer's service a legitimate response or retaliation? (iii) Should passwords have been redacted before publication, not after?

cases.summary: Paget's Black Hat DC talk on RFID security problems in HID access cards was pulled after a legal threat from HID, and the research was not published.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should a vendor be able to stop research on access-control cards protecting buildings? (ii) Does withholding RFID cloning research protect card holders or leave them unaware? (iii) Should an employer pull a talk to avoid litigation costs?

cases.institution: David Maynor & Robert Graham (Errata Security) / TippingPoint
cases.summary: Errata Security reverse-engineered TippingPoint's intrusion-prevention rule set to identify the vulnerabilities the rules protected against, drawing a threat from TippingPoint. The bulk of the research was later published at Black Hat 2007.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Deriving unpatched vulnerabilities from a vendor's protection signatures: defensive research or zero-day harvesting? (ii) Does publishing the method endanger customers relying on those rules? (iii) Can IPS vendors keep signatures confidential without slowing defense?

cases.summary: Two researchers reported a SQL injection flaw in the SimpleBlog Drupal theme and were threatened with legal action the same day. Two days later they released an exploit on Exploit-DB.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is releasing an exploit two days after a legal threat retaliation or protection of users? (ii) Should a threat end a researcher's duty to coordinate? (iii) How should small open-source theme authors handle reports they don't understand?

cases.summary: Sybase threatened NGSSoftware over planned publication of database vulnerabilities. The threat was dropped and the research published.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should database customers learn about flaws even when the vendor objects to timing? (ii) Do license terms limit what researchers can say about benchmarked or tested software? (iii) Does a dropped threat still chill other researchers?

cases.institution: Billy Hoffman & Virgil Griffith / Blackboard Transaction System
cases.summary: Blackboard sent a cease-and-desist to the Interz0ne conference and filed a complaint against two students who planned to present flaws in its campus card transaction system. The parties reached a confidential agreement.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should vendors be able to stop students presenting flaws in campus systems they use daily? (ii) Do confidential settlements protect students or bury research? (iii) Does a vendor's repeated conflict with student researchers (see also Demirkapi) suggest a pattern worth weighing?

cases.summary: Auriemma published vulnerabilities in the Unreal game engine and received a legal threat from Epic Games. The same day, Epic's Mark Rein apologized publicly, calling it a 'moment-of-stupidity' reaction.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Does a quick public apology repair the chilling effect of a threat? (ii) Should game engines used by millions be held to enterprise disclosure norms? (iii) Should researchers coordinate with game vendors before publishing?

cases.summary: HP invoked the DMCA in threatening SNOsoft over a Tru64 Unix vulnerability. The two later agreed on a disclosure timeline, and additional Tru64 vulnerabilities were published.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should copyright law apply to publishing an operating system vulnerability? (ii) Is a negotiated timeline after a threat a fair outcome? (iii) Did using the DMCA here set a precedent that helped or hurt the field?

cases.summary: Tena published research showing weaknesses in Tegam's Viguard antivirus, contradicting its marketing claims. Tegam pursued him in French courts, which imposed a suspended fine of 5,000 euros.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should reverse engineering to test a security product's claims be treated as copyright infringement? (ii) Do consumers' interests in accurate antivirus marketing outweigh vendor IP? (iii) How should researchers in stricter jurisdictions publish product evaluations?

cases.summary: A researcher reported authentication vulnerabilities in Wowza's media server; the vendor threatened to 'reevaluate' his independent consultant status, among other indirect threats. He disclosed after the vendor refused a remediation plan and left its consultant program. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
cases.dilemmas: (i) When a researcher also earns income from the vendor, can disclosure decisions stay independent? (ii) Is threatening someone's business relationship a legal threat by another name? (iii) Should a vendor's refusal to share a remediation plan trigger disclosure?

cases.summary: Miller found vulnerabilities in the Android-based T-Mobile G1, which Google downplayed. Years later he said Google went to his employer, later clarifying it was not a legal threat but a lecture on responsible disclosure to his boss. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is contacting a researcher's employer a legitimate complaint or indirect pressure? (ii) Did speaking to the press before a patch serve G1 users? (iii) Where is the line between lecturing and threatening?

cases.summary: Edge reportedly rescinded a Black Hat talk on FileVault encryption weaknesses after Apple invoked an existing NDA. Black Hat's CFP team found no record of the talk being submitted, and Attrition suggested the incident was used for publicity. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should an NDA with a vendor override disclosure of flaws affecting all users? (ii) How should the community treat suppression claims that may be publicity? (iii) Should researchers under NDA research that vendor's products at all?

cases.summary: Argeniss planned to publish one Oracle database vulnerability a day for a week to pressure Oracle over slow patching, then cancelled amid rumors of financial or legal threats. disclose.io lists this as unconfirmed.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is a public 'bug a day' campaign legitimate pressure or reckless exposure of customers? (ii) Should frustration with a vendor's patch speed justify releasing unpatched flaws? (iii) Do rumored threats chill research as much as real ones?

cases.summary: A student used keyloggers on university computers to collect other students' credentials in order to expose security weaknesses, and was charged with computer crimes. disclose.io lists this among incidents that crossed the line.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Can collecting real users' credentials ever be justified to prove a system is insecure? (ii) Does a good motive excuse harm to classmates who never consented? (iii) What should a student do when an institution ignores warnings?

cases.summary: Grutzmacher reported SNMP flaws in H3C and Huawei networking gear to US-CERT on August 6, 2012, and told the vendors they had until his ToorCon talk. Days before the conference, HP, H3C's parent company, asked him not to present because it was not ready; he agreed to cancel. HP published its advisory on October 22, and Grutzmacher published his findings the next day.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should researchers honor a polite vendor request to cancel when the vendor had months of notice? (ii) Was the request about protecting users or about the vendor's own timing? (iii) Does agreeing to cancel set an expectation that makes future requests harder to refuse?

cases.institution: Sergey Gordeychik & Denis Baranov (Positive Technologies) / SCADA
cases.summary: The researchers' DEF CON 20 talk, 'SCADA Strangelove: How I Learned To Start Worrying And Love The Nuclear Plants,' promised about 20 new vulnerabilities in SCADA systems including Siemens SIMATIC WinCC. They pulled it about a week before the conference and it was replaced with another talk; no reason was given, and reporters speculated about vendor pressure. They later presented SCADA Strangelove research at 29C3 in December 2012.
cases.dilemmas: (i) How much industrial-control vulnerability detail, and what tools, are safe to release at a hacker conference? (ii) How should the community interpret a cancellation with no stated reason? (iii) Should ICS findings go through national CERTs and vendors before any public talk?

cases.institution: Riley Hassell & Shane Macaulay / Google Android
cases.summary: The Privateer Labs researchers did not appear for their scheduled Black Hat 2011 talk, 'Hacking Androids for Profit.' Hassell later said they withdrew to prevent an unacceptable window of risk to consumers and to make sure prior research was credited, and that they had alerted Google. Google said the identified bugs were not present in Android.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is withdrawing a talk over misuse fears responsible, or does it leave users uninformed? (ii) How should researchers handle discovering their work overlaps prior research? (iii) What should a vendor's public denial mean for the research's credibility?

cases.institution: Dillon Beresford & Brian Meixell (NSS Labs) / Siemens & DHS
cases.summary: Beresford and Brian Meixell pulled their TakeDownCon 2011 talk on Siemens PLC vulnerabilities after Siemens and DHS's ICS-CERT raised concerns; Siemens had found at the last minute that its planned mitigation did not work. Both researchers and NSS Labs said they were asked, not forced. Beresford presented the research at Black Hat in August 2011.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should government concern about critical infrastructure override a researcher's publication plan? (ii) Is voluntary withdrawal after an official request different from censorship? (iii) When a vendor's fix fails at the last minute, who should decide whether the talk goes ahead?

cases.summary: Initial reports said ATM vendors threatened Chiesa into cancelling a Hack in the Box Europe talk. Chiesa said no threats were made and the cancellation was logistical; some in the industry called it a publicity stunt.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) How should media and the community verify suppression claims before amplifying them? (ii) Does publicity-driven framing harm researchers who face real threats? (iii) Should ATM research be presented publicly at all before banks patch?

cases.summary: Juniper Networks pulled Barnaby Jack's Black Hat 2009 talk, 'Jackpotting Automated Teller Machines,' after the affected ATM vendor said its customers were not yet protected; Jack had reportedly worked with the vendor for months. After moving to IOActive, he demonstrated ATM jackpotting attacks at Black Hat 2010; Triton said it had patched in November 2009.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is a one-year delay a reasonable trade for giving operators time to patch ATMs? (ii) Should an employer, rather than the researcher, decide when a talk is ready? (iii) Does a live jackpotting demo inform defenders or instruct criminals?

cases.institution: Harvard University Facebook Messenger -- Aran Khanna
cases.summary: student developed a chrome extension called "marauders map" used location coordinates already attached to facebook messenger messages to map movements released the extension to the public showing the privacy issue didn't consult facebook, FB asked to remove it and withdrew his internship facebook changed location sharing behavior no arrests/charges
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is it ethical to expose people's location just to demonstrate a privacy issue? (ii) Was publicly releasing the extension necessary? (iii) Is Facebook justified in withdrawing his internship? (iv) Is collecting existing data ethically different from creating new surveillance capabilities?

cases.summary: Crypto AG was a Swiss company selling encryption devices to governments around the world it was secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence (BND) devices were rigged so the agencies could read customers’ “secure” communications customers thought they were buying neutral, trustworthy equipment exposed in 2020 through a Washington Post / ZDF / SRF investigation of a leaked CIA history reporting says the intel was valuable, but agencies also saw abuses by some customer governments and did not act
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is deceiving customers acceptable for national security? (ii) Should intelligence agencies act on what they learn about human rights abuses, or protect the source? (iii) Does a case like this damage trust in all encryption vendors?

cases.summary: the FBI, working with Australian police, secretly ran an encrypted-phone company called ANOM the phones were marketed to criminal groups through underworld distributors every message was quietly copied to law enforcement the operation ran for about three years and was announced in June 2021 led to hundreds of arrests across many countries the FBI got access to messages outside the US through a third country’s cooperation, which was a legal workaround
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable for police to run a deceptive “secure” product? (ii) Should agencies be able to route around domestic legal limits through foreign partners? (iii) Does this make people less willing to trust real privacy tools?

cases.summary: malware discovered in 2010 that targeted specific industrial control systems widely attributed to the US and Israel, though neither has officially confirmed it aimed at centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility it spread beyond its target through Windows vulnerabilities and USB drives used several zero-day exploits showed that software can cause physical damage
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is a cyberattack on infrastructure different from a conventional strike? (ii) Is it acceptable to hoard and use zero-days that leave everyone else vulnerable? (iii) Who is accountable when the code escapes its target?

cases.summary: in 2016-2017 a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers leaked tools linked to the NSA the leak included the EternalBlue exploit for Windows reporting says the NSA had known about the flaw for years and had not told Microsoft Microsoft patched it in March 2017 and the leak came a month later EternalBlue was then used in WannaCry (2017) and NotPetya many systems stayed unpatched, so harm continued
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.outcome: No charges filed for the leak itself
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should governments keep zero-days for intelligence or disclose them to vendors? (ii) Who is responsible for the harm the leaked exploit caused? (iii) How should exploit retention be overseen?

cases.institution: Apple vs. FBI / San Bernardino iPhone
cases.summary: after the 2015 San Bernardino attack, the FBI recovered an iPhone used by one of the attackers the phone was locked and could erase its data after repeated wrong passcodes in February 2016 a court ordered Apple to help the FBI get around those protections Apple refused, arguing it would have to build a weakened version of its own software the FBI later said an outside party had unlocked the phone and dropped the case
cases.outcome: FBI withdrew court order after third-party access
cases.dilemmas: (i) Can a company be forced to weaken its own security? (ii) One phone vs. every user’s security: what responsibility does the outside party that unlocked it have?

cases.summary: in July 2021 the REvil ransomware group exploited Kaseya’s VSA remote-management software the malicious update was pushed through managed service providers (MSPs) to their downstream customers, including many small businesses researchers at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) had reported the vulnerability to Kaseya in good faith before the attack Kaseya was reportedly still working on a patch when the attack happened the FBI reportedly had access to REvil’s infrastructure and obtained a decryption key but held it back for about three weeks the reported reason was to avoid tipping off REvil while planning a disruption operation, while victims stayed locked out REvil’s servers went offline shortly after, and Kaseya later got a key from a third party
cases.outcome: Ransomware incident; recovery and law-enforcement actions
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should law enforcement hold back a decryption key to pursue the attackers, or give it to victims right away? (ii) How long is too long for a vendor to fix a vulnerability that researchers reported in good faith? (iii) Who decides whose harm counts more: current victims or future ones?

cases.summary: in early 2021 attackers (Microsoft attributed it to a China-linked group, Hafnium) exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in on-premises Exchange servers they planted web shells that gave persistent access, and other groups piled on after the vulnerabilities became public Microsoft released patches, but many organizations were slow to apply them or did not know they were compromised patching did not remove web shells that were already installed in April 2021 the DOJ got a court order to have the FBI copy and remove web shells from hundreds of vulnerable US servers owners did not consent beforehand and were notified afterward
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should the government be able to access private systems without consent to fix a security problem? (ii) Who is responsible for cleanup when owners cannot or will not do it? (iii) Does a court order make it ethical if owners are not told first?

cases.summary: on July 19, 2024 CrowdStrike pushed a faulty content update to its Falcon sensor on Windows machines millions of machines crashed into boot loops, disrupting airlines, hospitals, banks, and emergency services the cause was a software error in a rapid-response content update, not an attack the update went to all customers at once rather than in stages fixes required manual repair on many machines, so recovery took days CrowdStrike published a root-cause analysis and promised staged rollouts and more testing scammers also exploited the confusion with fake fixes
cases.dilemmas: (i) Should security vendors be liable for outages their products cause? (ii) Does deep system access by security tools create too much risk for the protection it gives? (iii) How fast should urgent security updates ship vs. how carefully should they be tested?

cases.summary: EncroChat sold modified phones with encrypted messaging, marketed as private French and Dutch authorities got into the network and installed malware on the devices, reportedly in 2020 they collected messages from tens of thousands of users, which led to thousands of arrests across Europe the data was shared with other countries’ police defendants challenged the evidence, arguing it was intercepted illegally courts in several countries mostly allowed the evidence, but debate continued the French operation’s technical details stayed secret
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable to hack every user of a service if most are suspected criminals? (ii) Should defendants be able to challenge evidence when the technique stays secret? (iii) What happens to legitimate users caught up in the operation?

cases.summary: Heartbleed was a flaw in OpenSSL's heartbeat extension that could allow attackers to read portions of server memory, potentially exposing credentials, session data, and private keys.
cases.dilemmas: (i) What obligations do maintainers of widely deployed security libraries have when their project is underfunded? (ii) How should organizations and funders distribute responsibility for software that is free to use but critical to security?

cases.summary: in late 2021 a critical remote-code-execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) was disclosed in the Log4j logging library it was reported privately to Apache by a researcher at Alibaba Cloud, and the fix was being developed when exploitation began in the wild Log4j is maintained by volunteers and was embedded in a huge number of products organizations struggled just to find where they used it maintainers worked through the holidays on multiple patches as follow-up flaws appeared the vulnerability was exploited widely within days
cases.dilemmas: (i) Who should bear responsibility for flaws in widely used volunteer-run software? (ii) Should disclosure be delayed, or sped up, once exploitation starts? (iii) What do companies owe the open source projects they depend on?

cases.summary: in 2017 WikiLeaks began publishing “Vault 7,” documents describing CIA hacking tools and techniques the material covered exploits for phones, computers, and smart TVs WikiLeaks said it withheld some code and redacted parts, but the documents still described capabilities in detail the CIA said the leak harmed its operations and security a CIA software engineer was later convicted for leaking the material to WikiLeaks supporters said the public should know about government hacking, critics said the disclosure helped adversaries
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.outcome: Criminal prosecution of source; public disclosures
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is publishing details of government hacking tools in the public interest or a security risk? (ii) How much should a publisher redact? (iii) Is the leaker a whistleblower or a criminal?

cases.summary: in 2013 Snowden, a contractor, gave journalists classified documents about US surveillance programs the documents described programs that collected phone metadata and internet communications at large scale he went to the press rather than using internal channels, saying those would not work the disclosures led to public debate and some legal and policy changes he was charged under the Espionage Act and has lived abroad, in Russia, since critics say the leak harmed intelligence work and that he went beyond exposing wrongdoing
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.outcome: Charges filed; Snowden remains in exile
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is breaking secrecy obligations justified when the programs may be unlawful? (ii) Should he have used internal channels first? (iii) How should whistleblowers be protected, given there is no real public-interest defense under the Espionage Act?

cases.summary: in July 2015 a group calling itself the Impact Team stole user data from Ashley Madison, a dating site for people seeking affairs they demanded that the parent company shut down the site, and published the data in August when it did not the leak exposed names, emails, and other personal details of millions of users users faced blackmail, public shaming, and reported harm to families and jobs the group framed itself as acting morally, objecting to the site’s practices journalists, researchers, and the public analyzed the leaked data, and some sites made it searchable
cases.outcome: Data published; litigation and extortion concerns
cases.dilemmas: (i) Is it acceptable to punish a company for its practices by exposing its users? (ii) Is it ethical for researchers and journalists to analyze or report on stolen personal data? (iii) Do people who used the service deserve less privacy protection?

cases.institution: Indiana University / Xiao Wang FBI Investigation
cases.summary: The workbook identifies this case for analysis but does not provide a short factual summary.
cases.intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
cases.outcome: Federal investigation reported; no arrest reported as of source date
cases.dilemmas: (i) Does funding from multiple sources create a conflict of interest? (ii) Would their research be ethically questionable? (iii) Should we look into how employees might be mistreated? (iv) What about cases where researchers face excessive retribution without some form of due process or procedural fairness?

cases.institution: Dennis Giese / Robot Vacuum Security Research
cases.summary: Security researcher Dennis Giese publicly documented reverse engineering of robot vacuum and connected-device ecosystems, highlighting privacy and security implications of cloud connectivity, firmware access, and smart-home sensors.
cases.dilemmas: (i) Owner Control vs. Vendor Restrictions: Should owners be free to modify or inspect device firmware despite warranties or vendor security controls? (ii) Security Disclosure vs. Exploit Proliferation: How much detail about device weaknesses should researchers publish when attackers may use similar methods? (iii) Smart-Home Convenience vs. Surveillance: What consent do household members and visitors give to connected sensors and cloud collection? (iv) Interoperability vs. Security: Can third-party firmware and research tools improve autonomy without introducing new vulnerabilities?

categories.name: Vulnerability Disclosure
categories.description: Cases centered on when, how, and to whom to disclose security findings — including responsible disclosure, media-first disclosure, non-responsive vendors, and provocation tactics.

categories.name: Informed Consent & Human Subjects
categories.description: Research conducted on people or communities without their knowledge or consent — phishing simulations, passive traffic monitoring, Tor de-anonymization, honeypots.

categories.name: Dual-Use Research
categories.description: Work that produces knowledge, tools, or methods usable for both defense and attack — ransomware simulations, keylogger research, internet-wide scanning, mass vulnerability databases.

categories.name: Legal Boundaries & CFAA Overreach
categories.description: Cases where good-faith or ambiguous research collided with criminal law, often highlighting disproportionate prosecution or vague statutory language (CFAA, DMCA, CMA).

categories.name: Institutional Suppression
categories.description: Cases where vendors, governments, or employers used legal, political, or economic power to silence, suppress, or retaliate against researchers exposing flaws or breaches.

categories.name: Financial Conflict of Interest
categories.description: Cases where research or disclosure was motivated or tainted by profit — short-selling, bug bounty disputes, threat-intelligence monetization, nonprofit commercial data deals.

categories.name: Critical Infrastructure & Public Trust
categories.description: Research on elections, medical devices, transit, water systems, and power grids where findings carry societal risk beyond the technical, including potential to fuel disinformation.

categories.name: Surveillance & Offensive Tools
categories.description: Development, sale, or deployment of tools designed to compromise systems at scale — commercial spyware, government malware operations, cyber-mercenary firms.
